title: The Fiedler dimension of networks of networks: from fractal to small-world architectures
authors: Lorenzo Grimaldi, Andrea Gabrielli, Pablo Villegas
abstract: Is the relaxation of a modular network dictated by its modules or by the network that connects them? The answer fixes the time scales of diffusion, consensus, and synchronization, all set by the Fiedler eigenvalue. We show that, for bundled networks, the two levels act one after the other: a random walker must first escape from its module and then spread over the network that connects them. The equilibration time is the sum of these two times, the time needed to reach the base from inside a fiber and the relaxation time of the base, slowed down by the mass of the fibers. The consequences are unexpected. However large the modules are, a small-world core always imposes its own Fiedler dimension; the modules survive only as a logarithmic correction, which slows down equilibration and hides the true exponent up to sizes far beyond any real network. Effective dimensions measured on finite modular systems can therefore be systematically biased. We analytically work out all combinations of finite-dimensional and small-world bases and fibers, and compare them with numerically exact spectra of representatives of each category.
summary: This work analyzes the relaxation dynamics in modular networks by treating the system as a combination of a base network and attached fibers. It establishes that the overall relaxation time is additive, and crucially demonstrates that the underlying small-world structure dictates the asymptotic spectral dimension, potentially misleading measurements on finite samples.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the relaxation dynamics of a modular network are governed by the properties of the individual modules or by the connecting network structure.
main_result: The equilibration time is found to be the sum of the base relaxation time and the fiber trapping time, and the small-world core always imposes its own Fiedler dimension, biasing finite-size estimates.
method: The analysis uses spectral graph theory, focusing on the Fiedler eigenvalue ($\lambda_g$) derived from the graph Laplacian, and employs scaling arguments to compare different network growth regimes.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a 'bundled network,' consisting of a base graph to which multiple copies of a 'fiber graph' are attached at every node.
key_observables: Fiedler eigenvalue ($\lambda_g$), equilibration time ($	au_{eq}$), spectral dimension ($d_s$), and effective Fiedler dimension ($d_{	ext{eff}}^g$).
important_parameters: The ratio $x = 	au_{trap}/	au_B$ dictates whether the gap is base-controlled or fiber-controlled; growth parameters like $	heta$ are crucial.
main_assumptions: The series law for equilibration time ($	au_{eq} \simeq 	au_B + 	au_{trap}$) is assumed to be exact under certain spectral conditions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the series law for $	au_{eq}$ across various network combinations, and show how the effective dimension $d_{	ext{eff}}^g$ scales with the composition parameter $	heta$ for different base types.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical model (modular networks), deriving the series law for relaxation times, analyzing the crossover between base- and fiber-controlled regimes, and finally providing asymptotic scaling laws for the Fiedler dimension in various growth classes.
why_interesting: The concept of spectral dimension and relaxation time in complex, structured networks is highly relevant to understanding energy or information transport in disordered quantum systems or complex quantum architectures.
